claim_verdicts.evidence: OrderService.cs @ stage-1 lines 12-18: `CustomerId = customerId, PlacedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, Status = "new", Items = items,` inside `new Order { ... }` in PlaceOrderAsync(int customerId, List<OrderItem> items).

OrderServiceTests.cs @ stage-1: SetsStatusNew asserts `Assert.Equal("new", order.Status); Assert.Equal(1, order.CustomerId);` (lines 20-21). No line in the file passes PlacedAt to any Assert; the only PlacedAt occurrence is the Seed on line 49.
Lines 48-54: `repository.Seed(new Order { Id = 1, CustomerId = 1, PlacedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, Status = "new" });` ... `Assert.Equal("cancelled", order.Status);` is the only assertion.

Every [Fact] builds its own fakes: lines 14-15, 27-28 (`new FakeOrderRepository()`, `new FakeNotifier()`), 40 and 60 (`new OrderService(new FakeOrderRepository(), new FakeNotifier())`), 48+50. No field or static member holds a fake; `OneItem` is an expression-bodied property that returns a new OrderItem per call.

xUnit docs: "xUnit.net creates a new instance of the test class for every test that is run, so any code which is placed into the constructor of the test class will be run for every single test." Confirmed by running a probe class (3 [Fact]s, static ctor counter) on a git-archive copy of stage-1 with xunit 2.9.2: instances 1, 2, 3, one per test. Round 3: "values stored in each instance's fields are not shared" is correct for instance fields (static excluded by wording).

claim_verdicts.evidence: Probe on a git-archive copy of stage-1 (xunit 2.9.2): `Assert.Equal(1, 2); output.WriteLine("PROBE SECOND ASSERT REACHED"); Assert.Equal("x", "y");` reported only the first failure; the second line was never written. xunit.assert.xml: XunitException is "The base assert exception class". Lesson now says "normally ends the test", which leaves room for Assert.Multiple ("Runs multiple checks, collecting the exceptions from each one").

"Fast: ... Milliseconds." "Isolated: ... no dependencies on any outside factors" "Repeatable: ... The test always returns the same result if you don't change anything in between runs." "try to include only one Act task per test". On time: calls to `DateTime.Now` → "If the test suite runs on Tuesday, the second test passes, but the first test fails." Order: "the order in which unit tests run should _not_ matter". Randomness is not named; it follows from Repeatable.

System.Runtime.xml (net10.0): UtcNow "Gets a DateTimeOffset object whose date and time are set to the current Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) date and time and whose offset is TimeSpan.Zero." Date "Gets a DateTime value that represents the date component of the current DateTimeOffset object." Two UtcNow reads straddling 00:00 UTC give different .Date values.

Now hedged ("can do more harm"), matching the round-1 suggested text. .NET docs: "You should have a high level of confidence that your tests work, otherwise, you can't trust them. Tests that you don't trust, don't provide any value. When a test fails, you want to have a sense that something is wrong with your code and that it can't be ignored."

xunit.extensibility.execution 2.9.2, xunit.execution.dotnet.xml (T:Xunit.Sdk.DefaultTestCaseOrderer): "Default implementation of ITestCaseOrderer. Orders tests in an unpredictable but stable order, so that repeated test runs of the identical test assembly run tests in the same order." Not source order, so "does not promise to run tests in the order they are written" holds.

OrderServiceTests.cs @ stage-1 lines 33-34: `var sent = Assert.Single(notifier.Sent); Assert.Equal(order.Id, sent.OrderId);` — two sends fail Assert.Single, a wrong id fails Assert.Equal. SetsStatusNew (lines 11-22) never reads notifier.Sent and asserts only Status and CustomerId, so it still passes as long as notifier.Send (OrderService.cs:21) does not throw.

DefaultTestCaseOrderer: "Orders tests in an unpredictable but stable order, so that repeated test runs of the identical test assembly run tests in the same order." DefaultTestCollectionOrderer: "...run test collections in a random order." So stable order holds inside one class (one collection by default), not the whole run. Second half is correct: with a shared FakeOrderRepository (`order.Id = nextId++`), a test can pass alone and fail in the full run.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: xUnit keeps the order of the tests in one class the same between identical runs, but running one test on its own changes which tests ran before it, so the same test can pass alone and fail in the full run.

issues.quote: xUnit keeps the order the same between identical runs
issues.text: Too broad for xUnit 2.9.2. Only the order of tests inside a collection (by default, one test class) is documented as stable: DefaultTestCollectionOrderer "run[s] test collections in a random order" across identical runs. The lesson's case (one shared repository in OrderServiceTests) is inside one class, so the point stands once scoped. Round-2 issues (order "can change from one run to the next"; "the class's fields") are resolved.
issues.fix: Write "xUnit keeps the order of the tests in one class the same between identical runs, but ..." and update claim 12 text to say "within a test class".

issues.quote: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test
issues.text: xUnit is a tool name that is not in known_vocab and is never introduced here or in the prereq summary. The lesson leans on it twice (new instance per test; stops at first failing assertion), and quiz q2, q4 use it. I can guess it runs the tests, but I have to guess.
issues.fix: At first mention, add a clause: "xUnit, the test framework that runs `OrderServiceTests`, creates …".

issues.quote: The cancel test shows the same care in the arrange step:
issues.text: "arrange step" is jargon not in known_vocab and not defined. I do not know which lines of the test are the arrange step or that tests have named steps.
issues.fix: Replace with "in the lines that set up the test, before it calls `CancelOrderAsync`:".

issues.text: "green" (and "a red test" in section 6) is casual jargon for passing/failing that is not in known_vocab. I infer it from context but it is never said.
issues.fix: Write "leaves … passing (green)" at first use, and "a failing (red) test" in section 6.

issues.quote: And shared state makes a test depend on which other tests ran before it
issues.text: A flaky test fails with no code change. For shared state to cause that, the set of tests that ran before must differ between runs. The lesson never says test order can change between runs, so I cannot see why a shared repository makes a test flaky rather than always wrong. Quiz q3 option b depends on this.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after this one: "Tests are not guaranteed to run in the same order every time, and running one test alone changes which ran before it." (add it to claims).

issues.quote: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test, and each test in `OrderServiceTests` creates its own fakes, so nothing leaks from one test into the next.
issues.text: I cannot connect "new instance of the test class" to "nothing leaks". The missing step is that anything stored in the test class's fields is therefore fresh for each test. Without it the first half of the sentence reads as unrelated trivia.
issues.fix: Add between the two halves: "so values stored in the test class's fields are not shared between tests,".

issues.quote: More assertions in one test method means better coverage
issues.text: "coverage" is not in known_vocab. Read as plain English ("checks more") it works, so it did not stop me, but it may be a technical term I am missing.
issues.fix: Replace "means better coverage" with "checks more of the code".

issues.text: The diagram node says "no network", but the prose only says the test runs the class "with fakes underneath"; network is never mentioned in prose.
issues.fix: In the prose sentence on "fast", add "with fakes underneath instead of a database or network".

issues.text: `Seed` is a method of the fake I have not seen explained here or in the prereq summary. I guess it puts an order into the fake before the test, but the prose does not say.
